title: BorgWarner Appoints Rajesh Kalathur to its Board of Directors
summary: Read and download our latest press releases.
body_text: Auburn Hills, Michigan, July 31, 202 6 – BorgWarner Inc. (“BorgWarner”) announced today that Rajesh Kalathur has been appointed to its Board of Directors. “We are pleased to welcome Raj to BorgWarner’s Board of Directors,” said Alexis P. Michas, Non-Executive Chairman of the Board of BorgWarner. “Raj’s extensive global leadership experience across finance, information technology, operations, and sales will be invaluable to our Board.” Mr. Kalathur most recently served as President of John Deere Financial and Chief Information Officer of Deere & Company, a global leader in the production of agricultural, construction, forestry, turf, power systems, and other solutions, which he joined in 1996 and from which he retired in 2026. In these roles, he led Deere & Company's financial services business segment with more than $70 billion in assets and oversaw enterprise-wide global information technology and cybersecurity functions. Prior to these roles, Mr. Kalathur served as Deere & Company's Chief Financial Officer for more than six years. Mr. Kalathur holds a Bachelor of Science in Mechanical Engineering from the National Institute of Technology in Jamshedpur, India, a Master of Science in Industrial Engineering from the University of Alabama, and a Master of Business Administration from the University of Chicago’s Booth School of Business.

title: Conversational Banking Won’t Scale Without Strong Foundations
summary: Discover the data, architecture, and governance foundations that banks need to scale conversational banking safely and effectively.
body_text: For years, banks have invested in chatbots, virtual assistants, and, more recently, generative AI-powered experiences. Most efforts have focused on specific tasks: answering questions, supporting transactions, or automating service interactions. But as conversational banking evolves beyond a channel capability and into an enterprise capability, a more fundamental question emerges: Can your bank scale conversational banking safely, consistently, and responsibly? That’s the focus of my latest report, Prepare The Foundations For Conversational Banking . This report explores the data, architectural, governance, and operating model capabilities required to move from experimentation to enterprise-scale deployment. The Next Challenge Isn’t The Interface — It’s The Operating Environment Most banks no longer need convincing that conversational banking matters. Instead, they are grappling with how to expand beyond isolated pilots and disconnected deployments. This challenge stems from a fundamental shift in what conversational systems do. They are no longer limited to answering questions; increasingly, they interpret customer intent, orchestrate decisions, apply policies, and execute actions across journeys. As a result, weaknesses in data, architecture, or governance can affect not only customer experience but also customer outcomes, operational resilience, and regulatory compliance. In our previous report, Create Your Conversational Banking Roadmap , we argued that banks need a clear vision, strategy, and roadmap anchored in customer trust and outcomes. Conversational banking should not be pursued as a cost-reduction exercise alone. It must help customers achieve meaningful outcomes while reinforcing trust. But strategy alone is not enough. Banks cannot scale conversational banking if customer data remains fragmented, governance is inconsistent, or architectures cannot support secure execution across systems. That’s why the next stage of maturity requires banks to focus on foundations. Three Foundations For Enterprise-Scale Conversational Banking Our research highlights three interconnected areas that banks must strengthen to support conversational banking at scale. Data And Knowledge Foundations Conversational systems depend on access to accurate, contextual, and well-governed data and knowledge. While banks possess vast amounts of customer and operational data, these assets often remain fragmented across products, channels, and business units. The result is inconsistent experiences, limited context, and greater risk when AI systems operate across journeys. Leading banks are investing in: Data quality, lineage, and semantic governance. Unified customer context and customer 360 capabilities. Curated enterprise knowledge repositories. Secure execution layers that connect intent to authorized action. Without these capabilities, even sophisticated conversational interfaces struggle to deliver reliable outcomes. Secure Architecture And Decision Orchestration The future of conversational banking depends on orchestration. Banks need architectures that connect models, policies, enterprise systems, and human oversight in a controlled and repeatable way. Rather than operating as standalone applications, conversational experiences increasingly act as coordination layers across customer journeys. Key capabilities include: Omnichannel context continuity. Hybrid architectures that combine deterministic and generative approaches. Runtime governance and interaction memory. Modular, vendor-agnostic technology stacks. Risk-aligned decision orchestration. Governance And Operating Models Perhaps the most important finding from our research is that conversational banking should be managed as an enterprise capability rather than a technology project. As conversational systems become more autonomous, governance must be embedded from the outset. Accountability, risk management, compliance, and performance oversight need to be integrated throughout the lifecycle. Key elements include: Enterprise control planes and oversight mechanisms. Risk-based escalation and intervention processes. Continuous monitoring and model validation. Federated operating models that balance central governance with business ownership. Workforce readiness and operating model evolution. From Roadmap To Reality This report completes a three-part research series on conversational banking at a time when the industry is shifting from AI experimentation to execution. Our first report explored the evolution of conversational banking and emerging market dynamics. The second helped banks develop outcome-led, trust-based roadmaps focused on customer outcomes, trust, prioritization, measurement, and governance. This latest report addresses the next stage of maturity : As banks explore conversational systems that can increasingly reason, decide, and act across customer journeys, strong foundations become a competitive necessity. Read the report to understand what it takes to move from conversational AI experimentation to secure, enterprise-scale conversational banking. Banks that invest now will be better positioned to deliver intelligent, outcome-oriented banking experiences while maintaining trust, control, and regulatory confidence. title: Insurance at AI speed: Lemonade’s growth with AI decisioning
summary: If you think insurance can’t move at AI speed, meet Lemonade. The future of insurance marketing is AI first personalization, not louder discounts. This is how Lemonade used AI-decisioning to learn fast, cut regret from underperforming variants, and prove that friendly + speed beats “cheap + easy” for conversion.
body_text: If you think insurance can’t move at AI speed, meet Lemonade . The future of insurance marketing is AI first personalization, not louder discounts. This is how Lemonade used AI-decisioning to learn fast , cut regret from underperforming variants, and prove that friendly + speed beats “cheap + easy” for conversion. The mandate: conversions, not applause Lemonade’s goal wasn’t vanity metrics, it was more qualified renters-insurance requests . We used engagement (OR/CTR) for early signal, but success was defined by conversion and sessions tied to quote intent. We scaled quickly across new-lead and cross-sell campaigns - multiple content variations, carefully personalized across millions of users. Engagement wins came fast (double-digit CTOR lifts). Conversion didn’t automatically follow, and that friction became the work. The messy middle: where AI earned its keep What tripped us up: Regret from “clever” lines. Some brand-nice variants popped on OR/CTR but lagged on conversion. We kept a few alive too long, spending traffic we should’ve reallocated. Price-first framing didn’t work. “From $5/mo” nudged opens, but often failed to move purchase intent ; a few tests even lost conversion despite stronger OR. Convenience clichés underdelivered. “No hassle/instant” sounded smooth -average opens, soft conversions . Measurement gray zone. “Almost significant” p-values tempted quick calls. Reinforcement Learning needed clear separation to commit; we had to let windows mature. How we corrected course: Let the AI agents allocate harder and archive faster, reducing regret and freeing traffic for likely winners. Switched optimization from OR/CTR to conversion , accepting a longer stabilization window. The turn: clarity and time-to-value win A clear thesis emerged: friendly + speed converts; cheap + easy doesn’t. “ Friendly reminder: get renters insurance ” (human/social tone) sometimes pulled lower opens but delivered higher conversion —trust over tease. “ …in seconds ” (time-to-value) occasionally traded a bit of OR for meaningful conversion lift . Price-led lines and generic convenience claims lost steam at the decision step. As the bandit learned, allocation collapsed behind the top 1–2 variants, and fatigue-resistant replacements were predicted automatically. What actually worked Optimize to the outcome you’re paid for. Use engagement to explore; let conversion decide allocation. Shrink regret aggressively. Auto-archive non-performers; keep a small control; don’t spread traffic across “interesting” maybes. Lead with trust + time-to-value. Human tone (“friendly reminder…”) plus concrete speed (“in seconds”) beat price-first every time. Results (directional, portfolio-level) Multi-campaign CTOR lifts , with conversion gains concentrated in the friendly + speed thesis. Signature streams saw allocation consolidate behind those winning frames while unsubs stayed in check . Operating model shifted from manual overrides to always-on bandit learning: faster predict → approve → ship cycles and lower regret. What’s next Expand into deeper personalization across segments & smarter orchestration. Keep conversions as the north star; treat engagement as an accelerator, not the finish line. Adapt to the always-on world with AI, while continuing to lay out guardrails and brand guidelines. The human part This worked because the Lemonade team stayed disciplined when the data was ambiguous- choosing to learn , prune , and persist instead of chasing pretty metrics. Kudos to Patrick Barther’s CRM leadership and AI-forward thinking. The takeaway for insurance: AI isn’t just a feature; it’s an operating system for marketing decisions, and Lemonade shows the category can truly move at AI speed.
